title: Night Out

jokes.text: Michael has gum in his hair because he crawled under Stanley's car to inspect something shiny
jokes.setup: Michael appears disheveled and distressed at the start of the workday
jokes.punchline: He got on the ground and crawled under Stanley's car because something shiny caught his eye — revealing his impulsive, childlike behavior
jokes.explanation: The cold open gag works because it's perfectly character-specific — only Michael would ruin his appearance crawling under a coworker's car before 9am. The absurdity is grounded in recognizable Michael behavior: impulsive, oblivious, and creating his own problems.

jokes.text: "But, best-case scenario, you thought it was a quarter."
jokes.setup: Michael explains he crawled under a car for a shiny piece of tin foil
jokes.punchline: Jim's deadpan 'best-case scenario' reframe — the best he could hope for is that he humiliated himself for a quarter, not literal trash
jokes.explanation: This is a near-perfect Jim line. The economy is exceptional — one short clause reframes the entire situation and makes it worse in the most precisely calibrated way. It's character-specific (only Jim would twist the knife this perfectly), structurally tight, and gets a bigger laugh on rewatch when you realize he's essentially saying Michael's dignity isn't worth 25 cents. One of the episode's best moments.

jokes.text: "Kill me, right now."
jokes.setup: Jim points out that even the best-case scenario for crawling under the car was finding a quarter
jokes.punchline: Michael's melodramatic response to having his self-delusion punctured
jokes.explanation: Functional Michael melodrama. The line lands because of context and Steve Carell's delivery, but there's nothing novel about Michael saying 'kill me' — it's a reliable but unremarkable character tic.

jokes.text: Michael demands an ice cream sandwich for his hair; Jim clarifies the peanut butter is for the gum, not a snack, and it's 9am
jokes.setup: Jim offers peanut butter as a hair remedy
jokes.punchline: Michael's first instinct is to eat it, prompting Jim to clarify both the purpose and the hour
jokes.explanation: The 'it is 9:00 a.m.' tag is the best part — Jim's understated judgment lands the joke. Michael wanting to eat the remedy is on-brand and works, but is a fairly predictable beat.

jokes.text: "No, Dwight, not the good peanut butter. People are gonna get mad." / "Hey, hey, hey. This is my hair we're talking about."
jokes.setup: Dwight is sent to get peanut butter for Michael's hair
jokes.punchline: The office apparently has 'good' and 'bad' peanut butter, and Michael invoking the sanctity of his hair to justify using the premium supply
jokes.explanation: The implicit world-building (the office has tiered peanut butter) is funny and grounded. Michael's indignant defense is character-appropriate. Not a standout but a solid escalation of the cold open bit.

jokes.text: Dwight tasting the peanut butter from Michael's hair and noting the calorie content
jokes.setup: Peanut butter is being massaged into Michael's hair
jokes.punchline: Dwight tastes it — from Michael's hair — and evaluates it nutritionally
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Dwight — he tastes someone else's hair-remedy without social inhibition and pivots immediately to caloric analysis. The disgust from whoever says 'that's disgusting' grounds the audience reaction. Strong character moment that gets a genuine reaction.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head about dating: 'men are visual creatures' leading into his inability to name a famous artist
jokes.setup: Michael sets up a grandiose statement about men being 'visual creatures' who 'crave beauty like a piece of fine art by...'
jokes.punchline: He trails off, unable to name a single renowned artist, then recovers with 'any number of renowned artists'
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed talking-head bit. The setup (men crave beauty like fine art) promises intellectual posturing; the payoff is Michael visibly blanking on literally any artist's name. The recovery — 'any number of renowned artists' — is the perfect Michael move: doubling down with vague confidence. Pure character comedy executed through structure. The pause mid-sentence is where the joke truly lives.

jokes.text: "Or an arty photograph of Cindy Crawford nude."
jokes.setup: Michael pivots from 'fine art by any number of renowned artists' to describe what he actually finds visually appealing
jokes.punchline: His example of beauty/fine art is a nude celebrity photograph, framed as 'arty' to give it legitimacy
jokes.explanation: The word 'arty' is doing enormous comedic work here — it's Michael's attempt to class up his base aesthetic. The specificity of Cindy Crawford grounds it and the 'nude' tag is the punchy button. Works as a continuation of joke #7.

jokes.text: "They just lack a certain Crawfordness."
jokes.setup: Michael has been explaining that the women he's set up with have 'great personalities' but fall short of his aesthetic ideal
jokes.punchline: He invents the word 'Crawfordness' — using Cindy Crawford as a unit of attractiveness measurement
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Crawfordness' is a perfect Michael Scott neologism — it sounds like something a man of middling intelligence would coin to sound sophisticated, it's highly quotable, and it pays off the Cindy Crawford setup with maximum economy. The '-ness' suffix transforms a celebrity name into an abstract standard of measurement. This is exceptional character comedy writing: only Michael would say this, and it would be funny in any context.

jokes.text: Ryan's corporate visit framing: he's caused the entire branch to work Saturday, and Michael greets him as 'my favorite branch'
jokes.setup: Ryan has just been described as the reason everyone must come in Saturday; he's in trouble
jokes.punchline: Michael ignores all of that and beams 'My favorite branch!' — his loyalty to Ryan completely overriding any awareness of the situation
jokes.explanation: Michael's blind loyalty to Ryan is a running thread this season and works well here as a character beat. The joke is light but functional.

jokes.text: Ryan subtly threatening Jim after Jim reveals he told David Wallace about the website concerns at the Christmas party
jokes.setup: Jim casually mentions Ryan's boss already knows about Jim's concerns
jokes.punchline: Ryan's stone-faced 'Watch your back, Jim' followed by 'I'm just kidding' — which is clearly not a joke
jokes.explanation: The 'I'm just kidding' after a genuine threat is a classic comedic construction, and it works here because Ryan's Season 4 heel turn is well-established. The joke is also the darkest hint that Ryan is actually dangerous, which rewards rewatch. Good use of character context.

jokes.text: Michael's protective speech: defending Ryan from mockery including his 'height or his half-beard'
jokes.setup: Michael intends to defend Ryan from the staff's legitimate anger
jokes.punchline: In defending Ryan, Michael inadvertently names the specific mockable things (height, half-beard) that presumably nobody was thinking about
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured Michael moment: his attempt to protect Ryan introduces attack vectors that didn't previously exist. 'Half-beard' is a specific, sharp visual descriptor that doubles as a genuine observation about BJ Novak's appearance during this era. The joke lands because it reveals Michael's protection is itself a form of unconscious humiliation.

jokes.text: "When will that be? TBD."
jokes.setup: Ryan promises all problems will be solved in Dunder Mifflin Infinity 2.0
jokes.punchline: Asked when, his only answer is 'TBD' — the corporate non-answer that says nothing
jokes.explanation: Economy is nearly perfect — two letters deflate all the corporate bluster. Stanley's follow-up question makes Ryan's non-answer land harder. Solid satirical jab at corporate speak.

jokes.text: The Dunder Mifflin website was 'infiltrated by sexual predators' via its social networking feature
jokes.setup: Phyllis asks a vague question that's cut off; Ryan matter-of-factly confirms the resolution
jokes.punchline: The casual reveal that the company's social network was taken over by sexual predators — stated as a resolved bureaucratic nuisance
jokes.explanation: The comedic engine here is the gap between the severity (sexual predators) and the casual bureaucratic tone in which it's delivered. Ryan's corporate detachment makes something genuinely disturbing into a dry punchline. Strong dark-comedic writing.

jokes.text: "And then an older gentleman asks you, 'Boxers or briefs?'"
jokes.setup: Ryan is explaining the 'one-stop consumer experience' of chatting about music, elections, etc. on the paper company's social network
jokes.punchline: He illustrates the predator problem by seamlessly including a predator's question as if it's part of normal social networking
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely well-crafted dark joke. Ryan lists benign social activities — music, elections — and then drops 'Boxers or briefs?' from 'an older gentleman' as if it's just another data point. The specificity of 'boxers or briefs' (a classically creepy question) and 'older gentleman' (a polite euphemism for predator) make this land hard. The deadpan framing elevates it significantly.

jokes.text: "If I had created a website with this many problems, I'd kill myself."
jokes.setup: Creed says he doesn't understand what the fuss is about — he likes the site
jokes.punchline: An immediate pivot to 'If I had created a website with this many problems, I'd kill myself' — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: A quintessential Creed Bratton moment. The joke works on multiple levels: it's a non-sequitur (he just said he liked the site), it's delivered as casual self-reflection, and it's completely character-specific — Creed's blunt nihilism is a running source of dark comedy. The economy is exceptional. High quotability. This is exactly the kind of isolated Creed bomb that makes the show legendary.

jokes.text: Kelly's defense of Ryan: "I am not applauding sarcastically."
jokes.setup: Kelly insists she believes Ryan has done a very good job
jokes.punchline: She preemptively denies sarcastic applause — which of course implies that's exactly what she's doing, or would do
jokes.explanation: The self-undermining protest is a smart construction. Kelly insisting she's not being sarcastic in a way that only makes sense if she's being sarcastic, while simultaneously defending the man who dumped her. Good character integration.

jokes.text: "But now, at a time TDB, all of these problems will be in the past."
jokes.setup: Kelly is making a passionate defense of Ryan's website, echoing Ryan's corporate language
jokes.punchline: She says 'TDB' instead of 'TBD' — getting the acronym wrong while parroting it to sound impressive
jokes.explanation: A subtle callback that rewards attention — Kelly has absorbed Ryan's corporate jargon but mangled it, which perfectly captures her character. It's a quick joke that might slide past viewers on first watch, making it a nice rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: "You done good, kid. You done good."
jokes.setup: Kelly has delivered an impassioned, grammatically incorrect defense of Ryan's terrible website
jokes.punchline: She closes her speech with a patronizing 'you done good, kid' — grammatically wrong and completely undermining the defense she just made
jokes.explanation: Kelly wrapping up her speech with a patronizing and grammatically wrong 'you done good' is funny because it undercuts everything she just said — it sounds like something you'd say to a dog who learned to sit. Solid character beat.

jokes.text: Michael physically clinging to Ryan while begging for a girlfriend hookup in New York
jokes.setup: Ryan is trying to leave the office; Michael walks with him
jokes.punchline: Michael's desperate plea — 'I need a girlfriend so bad' — while physically restraining Ryan from leaving, and Ryan's repeated 'Let me go, Michael'
jokes.explanation: The physical desperation (clinging, 'let me go') combined with Michael's raw emotional neediness is classic cringe-comedy. Ryan's repeated 'Let me go, Michael' is a perfect reaction line suggesting genuine physical restraint. Works because it shows how Michael's loneliness manifests in social dysfunction.

jokes.text: "Would you have sex with Meredith? Do you think she'd keep it quiet?"
jokes.setup: Jim is presumably just sitting at his desk; Michael approaches
jokes.punchline: Michael's complete non-sequitur opening about whether to have sex with Meredith for loneliness relief — delivered as an earnest logistical question
jokes.explanation: The joke is built on both the inappropriateness of the question and Michael's complete earnestness. 'Do you think she'd keep it quiet?' is the funnier half — it shows Michael has thought this through practically, not just impulsively. Jim's response ('I'm gonna go to my desk') is likely an excellent reaction beat.

jokes.text: Jim's reaction to the Meredith question — 'I'm gonna go to my desk'
jokes.setup: Michael has just asked Jim to evaluate Meredith as a sexual option for loneliness relief
jokes.punchline: Jim's immediate, flat departure — the implication is he was already AT or near his desk, making it the perfect non-answer
jokes.explanation: Classic Jim exit from an uncomfortable Michael conversation. The economy is perfect — rather than engage, he simply announces departure. The humor is in the understatement of treating this moment as a minor inconvenience rather than the workplace violation it is.

jokes.text: "Jim, it's not the horniness, okay? It's the loneliness."
jokes.setup: Michael has just asked about sleeping with Meredith; Jim is walking away
jokes.punchline: Michael's distinction — it's not horniness, it's loneliness — makes everything exponentially sadder and funnier simultaneously
jokes.explanation: This is the emotional thesis of the entire episode delivered as a punchline. The joke works because Michael insists on this distinction after asking to have sex with a coworker in secret — the context makes the 'it's loneliness' claim simultaneously absurd and genuinely sad. It's funny and heartbreaking at the same time, which is the show's signature mode. One of the episode's best lines. High quotability, perfect character specificity.

jokes.text: Michael inviting Andy to New York, then immediately disinviting him because he's not single, then citing 'Curse of Three'
jokes.setup: Andy enthusiastically joins in on the New York plan, describing relationship woes
jokes.punchline: Michael rejects him first for not being single ('singles only'), then invokes the superstitious 'Curse of Three' as a backup rationale
jokes.explanation: Two jokes layered: Michael's superstition about the 'curse of three' as a legitimate reason to exclude someone is funny, and it escalates from a social excuse into magical thinking. Also good: Andy's complaint about 'more chain than ball' is a solid euphemism.

jokes.text: Andy: "Old ball and chain's been a lot more chain than ball lately, if you know what I'm saying." Angela is standing right there.
jokes.setup: Andy is being enthusiastic about joining the guys' night out
jokes.punchline: He complains about his girlfriend/fiancée to the group — and Angela (his girlfriend) is standing right next to him
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe construction — the 'I'm right here' tag from Angela is the payoff. The 'more chain than ball' line is a decent euphemism, and the cringe comes entirely from Angela's presence. The joke doesn't need much explaining; it's well-executed situational comedy.

jokes.text: Michael's exit speech: 'I am going to go get laid. Goodbye! With sex!'
jokes.setup: Michael announces he's leaving to 'catch his drift'
jokes.punchline: 'I am going to go get laid' — then after a beat adds 'With sex!' as if the clarification was necessary
jokes.explanation: The escalating redundancy of 'With sex!' is the joke — Michael clarifying 'got laid' as if the audience might have missed it. It's a perfect Michael move: over-explaining the obvious to sound confident. High quotability because it's such a cleanly stupid capper. 'Goodbye! With sex!' is a genuinely memorable line.

jokes.text: Jim's plan to work late to avoid Saturday — confessional: 'And they loved it. Because this is a group that respects good ideas. The one time a year they hear one.'
jokes.setup: Jim explains he caught everyone before they left and proposed working late to avoid Saturday
jokes.punchline: The tag: 'The one time a year they hear one' — Jim's wry acknowledgment that good ideas are rare at Dunder Mifflin
jokes.explanation: A clean confessional beat. Jim's self-aware sardonic humor about the office's general competence is well-delivered. The structure (build to 'The one time a year they hear one') is tidy. Not exceptional but solid Halpert.

jokes.text: The club is called 'Prerogative' — Michael calls it out excitedly as if it's significant
jokes.setup: Ryan's assistant has told them the club name
jokes.punchline: The club is named 'Prerogative' — an implicit Bobby Brown reference that Michael (and possibly Dwight) almost certainly doesn't get
jokes.explanation: The joke is ambient — the name of a nightclub called Prerogative as a throwaway pop-culture gag. Works for sharp viewers but doesn't hit very hard. Background humor.

jokes.text: Dwight calling the packed club a 'fire hazard'
jokes.setup: Michael is excited about the packed, lively club
jokes.punchline: Dwight's immediate instinct is a fire code violation complaint
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Dwight. His first reaction to a vibrant nightclub is a safety regulation concern. Economy is excellent (just two words), and the character specificity is high. Not a big laugh but a reliable chuckle.

jokes.text: "These women look like white slaves." / "No, they're just hot. Hotties."
jokes.setup: Michael and Dwight are surveying the club crowd
jokes.punchline: Michael's deeply uncomfortable description is immediately corrected by Dwight with a completely flat 'They're just hot. Hotties.' — as if this is a reasonable clarification
jokes.explanation: The cringe comes from Michael's unhinged description and Dwight's deadpan non-sequitur correction. It's edgy in a way that's consistent with 2008 Office humor, and the joke is ultimately on the two socially oblivious men. The delivery dynamic (Dwight correcting Michael) is funny but the underlying material is uneven.

jokes.text: Michael's digression about going to Cabo not to see poverty but for 'glamour'
jokes.setup: Michael is continuing to comment on the club's atmosphere and crowd
jokes.punchline: He pivots to a non-sequitur about Cabo San Lucas being 'Third World' and his disappointment that vacationing there means encountering poverty when he wanted glamour
jokes.explanation: Michael's oblivious privilege moment — complaining that a developing region has poverty — is mild cringe humor. It characterizes Michael's worldview well but isn't a particularly sharp or memorable beat.

jokes.text: Ryan's reaction when he sees Michael and Dwight: dramatically enthusiastic, then cut to him telling his NYC friends 'Thanks a lot, guys. Good job!'
jokes.setup: Ryan puts on a big show of being thrilled to see Michael and Dwight at his club
jokes.punchline: Immediately after, he sardonically thanks his friends for telling Michael where he'd be — revealing his enthusiasm was entirely performance
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition between Ryan's performed excitement ('I'm so psyched you're here!') and his immediate sarcastic aside to friends is a sharp character moment. It reveals Ryan's two-faced nature efficiently. The cut itself is the joke — great editing comedy.

jokes.text: The office is locked from the inside — Jim's plan backfires because the security guard wasn't told and Dwight locked everyone in
jokes.setup: The staff stayed late to avoid Saturday; now they're ready to leave
jokes.punchline: The security guard doesn't know they're there, AND Dwight locked the office from the inside when he left — they're trapped
jokes.explanation: The subplot setup is well-structured: Jim's good idea immediately creates a new problem. The reveal that Dwight locked them in from the inside (how? why?) is perfectly absurd. Phyllis's threat ('If I'm not in my bath with a glass of red wine in one hour, you're both dead') is the highlight of this beat.

jokes.text: Phyllis: "If I'm not in my bath with a glass of red wine in one hour, you're both dead."
jokes.setup: Jim and Dwight have accidentally trapped the office staff inside the building
jokes.punchline: Phyllis delivers a completely specific and domestic death threat about her bath ritual
jokes.explanation: This line is excellent. The specificity — not just 'I need to get home' but 'in my bath with a glass of red wine' — transforms a generic complaint into a vivid character portrait. The casualness of 'you're both dead' after such a domestic image is perfectly incongruous. It's Phyllis emerging as a fully realized character in one sentence. High quotability and strong rewatch value.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head about Dwight holding both master keys — 'If I'm dead, you guys have been dead for weeks'
jokes.setup: Jim explains there is a master key and a spare key — Dwight has both
jokes.punchline: When Jim asked what happens if Dwight dies, Dwight's answer was: 'If I'm dead, you guys have been dead for weeks'
jokes.explanation: The single best line in the episode. It perfectly encapsulates Dwight's paranoid survivalist worldview: the idea that if Dwight Schrute is dead, the soft office workers would have been dead for weeks already because they couldn't survive the threats Dwight faces daily. It's darkly funny, highly quotable, completely character-specific, and lands with perfect economy. This is a legitimately great sitcom joke — comparable to the calibration anchors at the 8+ level. Jim's delivery as a bewildered straight man makes it land even harder.

jokes.text: Dwight: "You resemble the Tolkien character." (about Troy the hobbit-sized friend) / Ryan: "He basically is, man. He's a regular banking wizard." / Dwight: "No, no, not a wizard. A hobbit."
jokes.setup: Ryan introduces Troy, his small-statured friend, trying to smooth over Dwight's bluntness
jokes.punchline: Ryan tries to redirect 'hobbit' to 'wizard' to make it sound like a compliment; Dwight corrects him pedantically — insisting on the accurate Tolkien classification
jokes.explanation: The joke has beautiful layering: Ryan's awkward attempt to spin 'hobbit' into 'wizard' (a more flattering Tolkien character), followed by Dwight's pedantic insistence on taxonomic accuracy — completely missing the social grace Ryan was attempting. Dwight's dedication to getting the Tolkien classification right over being polite is perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: Michael asks for chicken fingers and a Midori Sour at the bottle service; told no food served; orders cups of olives and maraschino cherries
jokes.setup: Bottle service arrives at the VIP table
jokes.punchline: Michael's club order is chicken fingers and a Midori Sour; when told there's no food, he requests two cups of garnishes as a workaround
jokes.explanation: The escalation from Midori Sour (a childish cocktail order) to a cup of olives and a cup of maraschino cherries is perfect Michael food behavior — he adapts the system to get some kind of snack at a nightclub. It's absurd and entirely character-driven. The specificity of the garnishes is what makes it.

jokes.text: Dwight asks Troy: "Do you live in a regular-sized house?"
jokes.setup: Dwight has just called Troy a hobbit to his face; Ryan is trying to smooth things over
jokes.punchline: Dwight's next question is whether Troy lives in a 'regular-sized house' — he's genuinely curious if the Tolkien parallel extends to the domicile
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and character integration. Dwight's follow-up question reveals he's not being deliberately rude — he's genuinely curious whether the Tolkien characterization is accurate down to the housing situation. The question is more absurd and funnier than any insult because it shows Dwight's literal, curious mind. One of Dwight's best moments in this episode.

jokes.text: Jim trying to call the security guard without knowing his name — 'Who have I got here?' / 'The African-American guy'
jokes.setup: Nobody in the office knows the security guard's name; Jim tries to call him anyway
jokes.punchline: Jim attempts to identify the guard by physical description on the phone: 'You're the African-American guy' — before eventually crowdsourcing his name incorrectly from the group
jokes.explanation: The cringe comes from watching Jim — normally so cool — flail through an embarrassing phone call while the crowd of coworkers guesses wrong names. The 'African-American guy' line is the most awkward moment. Works as sustained cringe with escalating guesses (Eddie, Evan, Hank, Edgar, Elliot).

jokes.text: The cascading wrong name guesses for the security guard: Eddie, Evan, Hank, Edgar, Elliot
jokes.setup: Jim is on the phone with the security guard and needs his name
jokes.punchline: Every coworker offers a different wrong name in rapid succession — nobody actually knows this person who works in their building
jokes.explanation: The escalating wrong guesses is a well-structured comedic beat — each new suggestion implies the previous person was completely wrong. It builds to Jim giving up and just calling him 'Chief' on the phone. The underlying joke (nobody knows the name of the person they rely on) is also a nice observational point.

jokes.text: Dwight tells Ryan's friends about weevil season on the beet farm: 'They lay their eggs inside the unripe beetroot, then, come springtime, the babies eat their way out.'
jokes.setup: Ryan's cool NYC friends are making small talk with Dwight about his beet farm
jokes.punchline: Dwight launches into a clinical description of weevil reproduction at a nightclub, delivered with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dwight context collision — agrarian agricultural knowledge deployed at a Manhattan nightclub. 'The babies eat their way out' is genuinely disgusting and delivered with pride. Ryan's friend's reaction ('That's too much for me, man') is the grounding response. Strong character comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight notices Troy has been to the bathroom several times and diagnoses a possible bladder infection, then offers to order cranberry juice
jokes.setup: Troy keeps disappearing to the bathroom — he has a drug problem Ryan doesn't recognize yet
jokes.punchline: Dwight diagnoses bladder infection and offers medical remedy (cranberry juice) at a nightclub, completely missing that Troy is doing drugs
jokes.explanation: Beautifully layered joke. The audience understands Troy is on drugs; Dwight sees only 'frequent bathroom trips' and applies his hypervigilant practical knowledge to diagnose a bladder infection. His solution (cranberry juice) is medically sound and completely insane for the situation. This is Dwight's dramatic irony at its best — his literal-mindedness applied to a scenario that requires the exact opposite of literal interpretation.

jokes.text: Hank (the security guard) says he'll be there 'in just under an hour' and the staff reacts with despair
jokes.setup: The staff is locked in and waiting for Hank to come let them out
jokes.punchline: Hank's ETA is nearly an hour away, crushing all hope of an early night
jokes.explanation: Functional escalation beat. The joke is the gap between hope (Hank's coming) and reality (in an hour). Works as a plot beat more than a comedy beat, though Phyllis's earlier threat gives it extra resonance.

jokes.text: The staff realizes nobody chipped in for Hank's Christmas tip last year — Jim was supposed to collect it
jokes.setup: Staff commits to giving Hank a big Christmas tip in gratitude
jokes.punchline: Multiple people admit they didn't chip in last year — because Jim was supposed to collect the money and presumably dropped the ball
jokes.explanation: A nice payoff: Jim's good-idea plan has backfired twice (locked in, now revealed as the reason Hank never got his tip), and someone connects those dots with 'Now he's never gonna come.' Good structural comedy — Jim's competence image takes two hits in one scene.

jokes.text: "Now he's never gonna come." — after revealing Jim didn't collect Hank's Christmas tip
jokes.setup: The group realizes Hank has reason to not rush to help them
jokes.punchline: Kevin's flat, definitive conclusion that Hank is now never coming
jokes.explanation: Kevin gets the button on a good escalating bit. The economy is excellent — one resigned sentence captures everyone's dread. Kevin's deadpan delivery is character-appropriate.

jokes.text: Andy shows the office his new back tattoo — Phyllis immediately says she considered a back tattoo too
jokes.setup: Andy apparently reveals a back tattoo
jokes.punchline: Phyllis immediately says she also considered one — and the show uses this to juxtapose Andy's excitement with Phyllis's unexpected identification with him
jokes.explanation: The visual gag (Andy's tattoo) can't be seen in transcript but Phyllis's declaration that she considered a back tattoo is the comedic beat — the unexpected image of Phyllis with a tramp stamp. Light but functional.

jokes.text: Andy's tattoo is 'Back to the Future' — 'Back' because it's on his back; 'Future' because he's the kind of guy who likes to look ahead
jokes.setup: Andy explains his tattoo choice
jokes.punchline: His 'deep' rationale for Back to the Future is a word-association chain: 'Back' = it's on his back; 'Future' = he's a forward-looking guy
jokes.explanation: This is genuinely great character comedy writing. Andy's 'logic' is self-satirizing — the audience can see the circular reasoning (he picked a title because of a word in it), and Andy is proud of the insight. 'Future, because I'm the kind of guy who likes to look ahead into the future' is delivered with complete sincerity. It's also the best possible tattoo choice for an Andy Bernard — a beloved 80s film he can explain intellectually but only at a childlike level. Highly quotable and distinctive.

jokes.text: Andy's tattoo artist has never heard of Back to the Future — Andy tells her to take a film education course
jokes.setup: The woman Andy is talking to doesn't know the film
jokes.punchline: Andy's condescending response — 'You should take a film education course' — delivered to someone who is presumably young and clearly out of his league
jokes.explanation: Good continuation of the Andy tattoo bit. Recommending a 'film education course' to a woman who doesn't know Back to the Future is peak Andy — simultaneously condescending and oblivious to the power dynamic of the conversation.

jokes.text: Michael says the club is 'like a sexy preschool' and wants a place to meet 'older women'
jokes.setup: Michael is uncomfortable with the young crowd at the club
jokes.punchline: He describes it as 'a sexy preschool' — trying to articulate why the demographic doesn't work for him
jokes.explanation: 'Sexy preschool' is a strong, original image that works as a Michael metaphor — only he would combine those words in that order. The follow-up (wanting to meet 'older girls') is a nice fumble (he says 'women' then 'girls'). Quotable phrase with good economy.

jokes.text: Michael approaches the Jersey State varsity basketball team — a group of very tall women — and calls them 'Amazons'
jokes.setup: Michael asked for older, taller women; he finds a group of tall college athletes
jokes.punchline: The group turns out to be the Jersey State varsity basketball team; Michael's immediate reaction is 'Amazons!'
jokes.explanation: Works as a visual punchline (clearly inferred from the dialogue). Michael's 'Amazons!' reaction is perfectly him — awed rather than intimidated. The joke sets up the subsequent physical comedy of Michael getting beaten up by the team.

jokes.text: The basketball players send Dwight a drink; Dwight immediately suspects poisoning and sends it back
jokes.setup: Women send Dwight a drink as a flirtatious gesture
jokes.punchline: Dwight's first and only thought is that it could be poisoned — 'Anything could have been in there. Nice try!'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character integration. Dwight's paranoid survivalist worldview applied to a romantic gesture is perfect — the social cue (a woman likes you) is completely overridden by threat assessment. 'Nice try!' is the button that reveals Dwight thinks this is an assassination attempt. This is a top-tier Dwight joke: it's funny, it's character-specific to an extreme degree, and it's impossible to imagine any other character doing this.

jokes.text: Dwight tells the woman he meets at the club that he 'washes dogs' — then clarifies 'That's one aspect of small pet grooming'
jokes.setup: Dwight is talking to a woman; she asks what he does
jokes.punchline: Dwight claims to wash dogs (Ryan advised lying about working in finance); the immediate correction — 'that's one aspect of small pet grooming' — is both more specific and worse
jokes.explanation: Ryan told the guys to say they work in finance; Dwight's attempt is 'I wash dogs' followed by an even more specific and unglamorous clarification. The comedy is in Dwight completely inverting Ryan's advice while also correcting himself to something worse. Strong character comedy with good economy.

jokes.text: Michael tells a woman he 'works in finance' (Ryan's pickup advice), while the woman tells him she washes dogs
jokes.setup: Michael is using Ryan's tip: 'tell women you work in finance'
jokes.punchline: The woman responds by describing her own job (dog washing) without pretension, while Michael is actively lying about his
jokes.explanation: A decent irony beat — Michael is lying about himself while genuinely charmed by a woman who's being honest about an unglamorous job. The underlying observation about dating performance vs. authenticity is present but not sharply enough executed to be exceptional.

jokes.text: Dwight's confessional: 'This needs to be shared.' — then a long pause before the next scene
jokes.setup: Dwight has apparently met someone he's excited about
jokes.punchline: His declaration 'This needs to be shared' to the camera, followed by apparent action — played as a sincere emotional moment from an emotionally repressed character
jokes.explanation: Short but effective talking-head — Dwight's emotional breakthrough is inherently funny because he's normally so repressed. The brevity is appropriate.

jokes.text: Dwight to Ryan: 'This needs to be shared.' — then Ryan sees Dwight has been narrating the weevil situation to Michael via text/radio
jokes.setup: Dwight is talking to Michael about something; Ryan approaches
jokes.punchline: 'This needs to be shared' — Dwight treating the weevil/beet farm content as urgent news worth broadcasting
jokes.explanation: A minor absurdist beat — Dwight's compulsion to share agricultural information extends to nightclubs. Context is somewhat ambiguous from the transcript alone, which limits the score.

jokes.text: Dwight's confessional: 'She washes dogs' / 'I don't want to get ahead of myself, but I think I want her to meet my mom.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is excited about the woman he's been talking to
jokes.punchline: The woman's profession (dog grooming) — the one Dwight himself pretended to have — is what makes him want her to meet his mom
jokes.explanation: A great structural payoff. Dwight lied that he washes dogs; the woman ACTUALLY washes dogs; Dwight now wants her to meet his mother. The cosmic comedy of Dwight finding his soulmate through a lie that turned out to be accidentally true is lovely. 'She washes dogs' delivered with reverent awe is perfectly crafted. Rewatch bonus because you need to remember the lie to fully appreciate the payoff.

jokes.text: Troy's monologue about nuclear holocaust and jungle tribes ruling the world — Ryan's 'Yeah, maybe' response
jokes.setup: Dwight is sharing his romantic excitement; Troy interrupts with an unhinged philosophical tangent
jokes.punchline: Troy's rambling theory about post-nuclear jungle warfare dominance is clearly drug-influenced; Ryan's one-word 'Yeah, maybe' response is the understated acknowledgment
jokes.explanation: Troy's drug-fueled paranoid monologue is implicitly funny as a comedy of recognition (who hasn't heard this at a party?), and Ryan's flat non-engagement is the right straight-man response. Works as character comedy for Troy and dramatic irony (Ryan doesn't yet know Troy has a problem).

jokes.text: Hank's phone call: 'Stop calling me, so I can put on my damn socks.'
jokes.setup: Jim is nervously checking in with Hank on his progress
jokes.punchline: Hank's exasperated request — he's trying to put on his socks and Jim's calls are slowing him down
jokes.explanation: Hank is a breakout bit character in this episode and this line cements why. 'Put on my damn socks' is such a specific, mundane detail — it makes the whole situation funnier because Hank is being perfectly reasonable (he's trying to get ready) while the office staff treat his grooming as an emergency. High economy.

jokes.text: Michael on his cell phone at the club talking to his mom about asking girls to dance and whether he shaved the back of his neck
jokes.setup: Michael is at a nightclub trying to meet women
jokes.punchline: He's calling his mother to report on his dating progress, reassuring her he shaved the back of his neck
jokes.explanation: A devastating character moment. Michael called his mom to report on his dating efforts, and the specific detail — 'yes, I shaved the back of my neck' — suggests his mother gave him pre-date grooming advice. This perfectly captures Michael's deep loneliness and arrested development. The 'I'm getting out there' as a report to Mom is heartbreaking and funny in equal measure. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Pam imagines Michael had planned 'Scrambled Egg Saturday'; Jim counters: 'More like, Hey everyone, let's get your boss laid Saturday'
jokes.setup: Pam and Jim are musing about what Michael had planned for the Saturday they're now avoiding
jokes.punchline: Pam's innocent 'Scrambled Egg Saturday' is immediately replaced by Jim's more accurate read on Michael's motivations
jokes.explanation: Pam's 'Scrambled Egg Saturday' is a nice piece of world-building — we can completely imagine Michael making people come in for a themed breakfast. Jim's corrective is efficient and accurate. The banter shows the Jim-Pam dynamic working well outside the main A-plot.

jokes.text: Jim's hypothetical: 'I bet Michael had some elaborate theme party planned, like Scrambled Egg Saturday.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are musing about what they're missing by not coming in Saturday
jokes.punchline: 'Scrambled Egg Saturday' — a made-up but completely plausible Michael theme so specific that it lands as a joke
jokes.explanation: The beauty of 'Scrambled Egg Saturday' is that it's immediately believable as a Michael event. The specificity — why scrambled eggs? why Saturday? — is exactly the kind of theme Michael would earnestly organize. It's an invented Michael joke that tells you more about Michael than many actual Michael lines.

jokes.text: Toby's talking head: 'I have an announcement to make. I am moving to Costa Rica.' — then he just hops the fence and jogs home
jokes.setup: The staff is locked in; Toby has apparently been building to an announcement
jokes.punchline: Toby announces he's moving to Costa Rica — then, having said it, immediately hops the fence and jogs away into the night. The 'announcement' was just him quitting and leaving.
jokes.explanation: The single funniest moment of the episode and one of the great Toby moments in the series. The structure is perfect: solemn announcement framing ('I have an announcement to make') followed by a life-changing declaration, followed by immediate action — hopping a fence and jogging away as if this was all planned. It perfectly captures Toby's repressed, desperate existence and his need to finally do something. The fence hop is a beautiful visual punchline. The absurdity of announcing a life change during a workplace lockout makes it iconic. This is top-tier Office comedy.

jokes.text: Michael's confessional after getting beaten up by the basketball team: 'Those girls really whaled on you bad.' / 'Why wouldn't they let me dance?'
jokes.setup: Michael apparently tried to dance with the women's basketball team and got beaten up
jokes.punchline: Michael's genuine bewilderment ('Why wouldn't they let me dance?') — he has no idea why this happened
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the basketball player setup. Michael's sincere confusion about why he was beaten up ('Why wouldn't they let me dance?') is the best part — he can't conceive of what he did wrong. Dwight's 'Do not take him to a hospital' suggests injury while also being absurd. Good cringe payoff.

jokes.text: Dwight refuses to go back in: 'I don't want to go back in.' / 'I know. Here we go.' — Michael's resigned acceptance
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to get Dwight to re-enter the club after being beaten up
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'I know. Here we go.' suggests he's accepting an unhappy situation with exhausted resignation — but it's unclear whether they're going back in or leaving
jokes.explanation: A softer moment that works more as character texture than a joke. The weary dynamic between Michael and beaten-up Dwight is mildly amusing but not a strong comedic moment.

jokes.text: Oscar suggests the cleaning crew can help them escape; Jim assumes they speak Spanish; Oscar corrects him; they do in fact speak Spanish
jokes.setup: The cleaning crew arrives; Jim immediately assumes they speak Spanish (and only Spanish)
jokes.punchline: Oscar (who is Latino) corrects Jim's assumption — then the cleaning crew answers in Spanish, making Jim accidentally correct
jokes.explanation: A smart structural joke: Oscar (the Latino character) calls out Jim's racial assumption, then the cleaning crew immediately proves Jim right — which retroactively makes everyone more uncomfortable. The tag 'Lucky us' is a perfect dry button. Oscar's moral authority collapsing at the exact moment of his correction is great structural irony.

jokes.text: 'They happen to speak Spanish. Lucky us.'
jokes.setup: Oscar corrected Jim for assuming the cleaning crew spoke Spanish; they immediately respond in Spanish
jokes.punchline: Jim's dry 'Lucky us' — acknowledging both that he was right and that being right here is embarrassing
jokes.explanation: Two words doing a lot of work. 'Lucky us' perfectly captures the cringe of being accidentally right in a racially uncomfortable way. The economy is exceptional. It functions as both Jim's relief and his embarrassment — a perfect dual-register line.

jokes.text: Ryan's apartment: one sofa, one floor; Michael and Dwight fight for the sofa while Ryan watches; Dwight offers to sing a lullaby
jokes.setup: Michael, Dwight, and Ryan return to Ryan's apartment after the club
jokes.punchline: Ryan has no guest bed — just a sofa and a floor — and the adult men argue over them like children; Dwight offers a lullaby from his sick bed repertoire
jokes.explanation: The regression to childlike behavior (fighting for sofa, lullaby offer) is a good visual for the Michael-Dwight dynamic. Dwight's concern about getting his head stepped on if he gets the floor is characteristically practical and funny.

jokes.text: Michael/Dwight fight over the sofa: 'I got the sofa.' / 'I got the sofa.' / 'Dwight, I got the sofa, I'm the boss.' / 'Come on! I got floor!'
jokes.setup: Ryan has offered the sofa and floor as sleeping options
jokes.punchline: Michael invokes his managerial authority to win the sofa; Dwight accepts the floor with defeated enthusiasm ('I got floor!')
jokes.explanation: A solid physical comedy setup resolved by Michael's invocation of the corporate hierarchy for a petty personal gain. 'I got floor!' from Dwight is funny because he pivots immediately to ownership of a lesser prize — his loyalty is total and his acceptance is instant.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'In case anybody needs to go to the bathroom in the middle of the night, I don't want to get my head stepped on.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has accepted he'll sleep on the floor
jokes.punchline: His reasoning for sleeping on the floor is purely practical/defensive — a contingency plan for bathroom trips — revealing he's immediately strategizing his floor position
jokes.explanation: Dwight instantly flips from competing for the sofa to tactically planning his floor position. His concern about being stepped on shows he's already doing threat assessments from ground level. Pure Dwight logic — always preparing for the worst-case scenario of any situation.

jokes.text: Dwight offers to sing Michael a lullaby; Michael refuses; Dwight: 'It's a lullaby.' — as though that settles the matter
jokes.setup: Michael refuses Dwight's offer to sing the lullaby his mother sang him when they were sick
jokes.punchline: Dwight's rebuttal is simply restating what it is — a lullaby — as though Michael's resistance to a lullaby is irrational
jokes.explanation: Brief but good. Dwight's literalism — the lullaby is called a lullaby, it is for sleeping, Michael wants to sleep, therefore the lullaby is appropriate — is a clean character joke. His genuine puzzlement at the refusal is the subtext.

jokes.text: Dwight offers to sing a sick-bed lullaby to Ryan; Ryan says no; Dwight persists
jokes.setup: Ryan is sick from drug use; Dwight offers comfort
jokes.punchline: The lullaby offer from Dwight to the hip young Ryan is deeply incongruous and inappropriately parental
jokes.explanation: Dwight parenting a miserably hungover/high Ryan is a nice role reversal. The offer of a lullaby is pure Dwight — old-world care methods applied inappropriately.

jokes.text: Ryan confessional: 'I think my friend Troy might have a drug problem. What do I do?'
jokes.setup: Ryan has been doing drugs all night
jokes.punchline: Ryan — himself clearly on drugs — expresses genuine concern about Troy's 'drug problem' with no apparent self-awareness
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is perfectly constructed. Ryan is on drugs; Ryan is worried about Troy being on drugs. His sincere 'What do I do?' to the camera, while visibly in a compromised state, is one of the episode's strongest moments. The joke also pays off Dwight's cranberry juice diagnosis from earlier.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'I think his species might have a higher tolerance than ours.'
jokes.setup: Ryan says Troy has a drug problem
jokes.punchline: Dwight's response is that Troy (the 'hobbit') might have a different biological tolerance because of his 'species'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best lines and an excellent callback. Dwight has genuinely classified Troy as a different species (hobbit) and is now making zoological-level assumptions about his biology. 'His species might have a higher tolerance' is funny because it's scientifically framed concern from someone who doesn't realize he's being absurd. The economy is excellent and the character integration is perfect — no one else would say this.

jokes.text: Michael's drug advice: tell Troy you're his friend, then put a wire on him to flip him into a snitch to catch bigger dealers — 'I've been watching The Wire recently. I don't understand a word of it.'
jokes.setup: Ryan asks what to do about Troy's drug problem
jokes.punchline: Michael gives elaborate law enforcement advice from The Wire — then immediately admits he doesn't understand the show
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top-three moments. Michael's elaborate Wire-derived advice is delivered with total confidence and surprising specificity ('flip him,' 'turn him into a snitch,' 'follow that guy to the people who're really, really bad') — and then demolished by 'I've been watching The Wire recently. I don't understand a word of it.' The admission undercuts everything he just said and reveals he's been regurgitating plot descriptions he can't actually parse. Perfect comedy construction: build authority, then reveal complete incompetence. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Michael's final confessional: 'Best night ever.' / 'It's not about the horniness. It's about the loneliness. And how can I be lonely with my boys?'
jokes.setup: Michael spent the night getting beaten up by basketball players, dragging Dwight to a club, sleeping on Ryan's floor
jokes.punchline: He declares it 'the best night ever' and revisits his loneliness thesis — finding genuine comfort in having his 'boys'
jokes.explanation: The episode's emotional button. The callback to 'it's not the horniness, it's the loneliness' lands because the episode has earned it — Michael's night was objectively disastrous but he found what he was actually looking for. The joke-that's-also-sincere is the show's signature move, and it works here. 'Best night ever' is funny because it's delusional, and poignant because it's also true.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Like a famous person once said, Boys on the Side. But I don't disagree. I say, Let's Hear It for the Boys.'
jokes.setup: Michael is wrapping up his thoughts about male friendship
jokes.punchline: He attributes 'Boys on the Side' to 'a famous person' (it's a 1995 Whoopi Goldberg film) — then offers his own alternative title as if these are competing philosophies
jokes.explanation: Characteristically Michael — citing film titles as philosophical positions, misremembering who said them, and presenting them as competing intellectual frameworks. 'Like a famous person once said' is a perfect Michael attribution. The pivot from 'Boys on the Side' to 'Let's Hear It for the Boys' (a Footloose song) is an accidental gender pivot that Michael doesn't notice. Good closing character beat.

jokes.text: Final shot: 'Son of a bitch.' — presumably Hank finally arrives to find the office empty
jokes.setup: Hank has been asked to come in after hours to let the staff out; the staff found another way out
jokes.punchline: Hank arrives to an empty office and delivers a perfectly timed frustrated expletive as the final beat of the episode
jokes.explanation: A perfect button to end the episode. Three words close a subplot that has been running through the entire B-story: Hank was asked to come in, made the trip, and found nobody. 'Son of a bitch' is the exact right response — not elaborate, not explained, just pure exasperation. Economy is essentially perfect. This is what a great episode tag looks like: funny, earned, and character-illuminating (Hank is a real person with feelings who just wasted his evening for nothing).

jokes.text: Final shot: someone (likely Creed or Kevin) walks into the office the next morning to find everyone still there — or an employee discovers the Saturday situation
jokes.setup: The episode has established all the Scranton employees worked late to avoid Saturday
jokes.punchline: 'Son of a bitch.' — the final line, delivered flat, as the last ironic beat on the evening's events
jokes.explanation: A functional episode button — three words that serve as the final ironic stamp on the evening. Without more context (who says it, what exactly they see), it's hard to score higher, but the economy is strong and it lands as a closing joke.

tmdb_overview: Ryan returns to Scranton but not to a warm welcome. He is making everyone in the branch come in on a Saturday to re-enter data into the new website. Michael makes it clear that Ryan is the reason they have to come in on the weekend. The rest of the staff aren't happy knowing a computer will be getting credit for all of their sales.
